newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon knew about torture manuals, Kennedy says.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon knew about torture manuals, Kennedy says.

text.p: The Pentagon was aware that training manuals for Latin American soldiers advocated murder, torture and extortion to put down insurgents, Representative Joseph Kennedy said Thursday.

The Massachusetts Democrat released a 20-page report contradicting an internal Defence Department Inspector General's report released last month that found U.S. military officials did not know the contents of the manuals.
Kennedy said he will propose legislation to prohibit the U.S. government from distributing such material.

He called for closing down the U.S. Army's School for the Americas at Fort Benning, Georgia, where the manuals were used by American instructors in training Latin American soldiers between 1987 and 1992.
The U.S. Army has trained about 60,000 soldiers from Latin American countries over the last 50 years at the school.

The report said two Army instructors there complained to their superiors that some things in the seven training manuals violated official U.S. policy, contradicting the Pentagon's report that it was unaware the manuals contained instructions prohibited by U.S. policy.
Kennedy's report also concluded the manuals had been approved by the Pentagon in the 1980s. The Pentagon report said the material had not been properly reviewed.

All the materials used to write the manuals were written in English, the Kennedy report said. That contradicted the Pentagon's version, which said the material was prepared in Spanish and therefore not readily understandable to officials in charge.
The manuals, similar to ones used by the CIA in the same period, were recalled in 1992.
Kennedy said the manuals "were one piece of a larger problem" and that U.S. officials believed that rules did not matter.
A Pentagon spokesman, Commander Joe March, said "this is largely a historical matter and the subject of historical research."
"U.S. policy is very clear," he said. "The things brought up ... are certainly prohibited."
He said that little documentation from the period in question exists and the Pentagon has been reviewing what still exists at the request of the National Archives.

Another spokesman, Captain Mike Doubleday, said at a Pentagon briefing that the manuals were distributed on request to embassies and military groups so "we don't know the extent to which the materials were actually used by individual countries down there."

"Steps have been taken to put into effect a system which would prevent this kind of thing from happening in the future, steps were taken back in the early 1990s to get rid of the material, to withdraw it from circulation," he said.
